title: Relations with the musicians' union and New York Local 802
summary: Lovett had no union trouble, and Smith describes the union man waiting in the wings at the Waldorf.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, how have your relations been with the union over the years? I know you've traveled a lot, going into different locals with the band. How have your relations been with the musicians' union? Do you have any complaints?
No complaints at all.
They had no complaints with you either?
No, no. There used to be a tough man in New York. What's his name?
(Inaudible). Petrillo.
No, he's in Chicago.
No. Well anyway --
Local 802?
Yeah, 802. Anyway but we didn't have any trouble. Julia and I went there and we didn't have any trouble at all.

I can remember taking a trio from Philadelphia to the Waldorf in New York and we're playing there in the grand ballroom and I looked to my left and there was a guy standing in the wings with his arms folded across
his chest and nobody had to tell me who he was. He was the sergeant at arms I guess -- he was a very nice guy but they don't miss a trick in New York, do they?
No.
Once you're in there they're on you -- not on you -- I don't mean that way but with you every second. They know --
If you're right.
-- exactly how much you owe them.
If you're right.
Well if you're not right, you're not going to play.
No, that's right.

But I looked in the wings and there he was, making sure, you know, how long we played, how much money, he got his check and so on. Anyway, so you've had no problems that way, there's no incidents or anecdotes you want to tell about these people?
No, no.
How about you, Crook?
I didn't have any trouble at all.
